sentences.text: Mamenchisaurus is distinguished by an exceptionally long neck that makes up nearly half of the animal's total body length.
Most Mamenchisaurus species measured roughly 15 to 26 meters in length, possibly up to 35 meters based on undescribed vertebrae.
The type species M. constructus, known from a single skeleton, is estimated to be between 13 and 15 meters long.
The holotype of M. hochuanensis included an almost complete vertebral column with 19 cervical, 12 dorsal, four sacral, and 35 caudal vertebrae.

M. sanjiangensis is distinguished from other species by an additional depression on posterior cervical and anterior dorsal vertebrae and a distinct arrangement of the spinodiapophyseal lamina on the third through seventh dorsal vertebrae.
Until 1994, the neck of Mamenchisaurus hochuanensis was among the longest known, though it was shorter than the previously known Supersaurus neck.
Researchers believe the fused tail vertebrae with expanded neural arches might have functioned as a club or sensory organ.
The genus Mamenchisaurus was established by Young in 1954.
The type species Mamenchisaurus constructus was named in 1954 by Professor C. C. Young.
The species Mamenchisaurus hochuanensis was described in 1972 by Young and Xijin Zhao.
The species Mamenchisaurus sinocanadorum was named in 1993 by Dale Russell and Zhong Zheng.
Mamenchisaurus fossils have been found in the Sichuan Basin and Yunnan Province in China.
All species of Mamenchisaurus were herbivores.
Chisel-shaped teeth were likely useful for stripping needles or leaves from branches and for biting fruiting bodies like seed ferns.
Bone histology analysis estimated that a Mamenchisaurus individual died at 43 years of age.
Analysis of M. youngi suggests its neck was almost straight in neutral posture, with slight upward bending at the base and downward bending near the head.
Research suggests the neck of M. youngi was kept mostly straight, except possibly at the base and near the head.
Manual analysis of cervical vertebrae mobility showed that the base of the neck could bend strongly upward.
The first cervical vertebra could curve 20 degrees relative to the second, and the fifteenth could bend backward 105 degrees relative to the rear.
Christian believed the neck usually held the head between ground level and an angle of more than 30 degrees with the back.
The ability of the neck base to move strongly sideways via flattened articular protuberances suggests a long neck provided a wide horizontal range.
Current analyses indicate that Mamenchisauridae form a distinct, primarily Asian clade within Eusauropoda, outside Neosauropoda.
The type species of Mamenchisaurus is Mamenchisaurus constructus.
The phylogenetic position of Euhelopus is debated, with some studies placing it within Macronaria and others outside Neosauropoda grouped with Mamenchisaurus-like taxa.
Mamenchisaurus lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 163 to 145 million years ago, from the Oxfordian to Tithonian stages in what is now Asia.
Uranium-lead dating places M. anyuensis in the Suining Formation at 114.4 million years ago.
M. sinocanadorum was found in the Middle to Upper Shishugou Formation, which radiometric dating suggests dates to the Oxfordian, ranging from 158.7 to 161.2 million years ago.
A 2019 study suggested the formation containing M. anyuensis was no older than the Aptian, implying the genus may have persisted into the Cretaceous, raising doubts about its classification.
It is debated whether Mamenchisaurus held its neck horizontally or could erect it like a giraffe to reach higher altitudes.
A recent biomechanical study suggests the neck was too immobile to erect due to very long cervical ribs, unlike diplodocids which had significantly more mobile necks.

A phylogenetic analysis suggested M. sinocanadorum is outside the clade of other Mamenchisaurus species and closely allied to Xinjiangtitan, but taxonomic action was refrained until M. constructus was re-evaluated.
The validity of transferring species from other genera to Mamenchisaurus is disputed by researchers.
The species M. gongjianensis is considered dubious.
